content: The healthcare industry, also referred to as the health profession, is a sector that encompasses individuals who apply their expertise, skills, and judgment to provide services aimed at maintaining or improving the health of individuals. It also includes the treatment and care of individuals who are injured, ill, disabled, or otherwise infirm. The delivery of modern healthcare relies on a growing network of trained professionals working collaboratively as an interdisciplinary team. The healthcare industry is one of the largest and fastest-growing sectors globally. In many developed nations, it consumes over 10% of the gross domestic product (GDP), making it a significant component of a country's economy. For instance, in the United States, healthcare expenditures accounted for 3% of GDP in earlier years, with projections showing an increase to 6% by 2016. In 2006, the total healthcare spending in the U.S. reached $2 trillion. According to Health Affairs, in 2007, an estimated $7,498 was spent per person in the U.S., accounting for 20% of all national spending. By 2016, this figure was projected to rise to $12,782 per person. A healthcare provider or professional is an individual or organization that delivers healthcare services systematically and professionally to those in need. The healthcare industry involves the provision of health services by these providers. Payment for such services is typically made by the patient or their insurance company. However, in some cases, healthcare services may be government-funded, as seen with the National Health Service (NHS) in the United Kingdom, or provided by charities and volunteers, particularly in less affluent countries. Healthcare delivery can take various forms in the modern world. The most common method is face-to-face interaction, where the care provider and the patient meet in person. This is the standard practice in general medicine across most countries. However, with advancements in telecommunications technology, remote healthcare delivery is becoming increasingly prevalent. This form of care involves communication between the practitioner and the patient through mediums such as phone calls, video conferencing, the internet, emails, text messages, or other non-face-to-face communication methods.
